title: Everyday foods from rainforests
keyIdea: Many foods we eat every day come from plants that first grew in rainforests, the hot, wet forests near the equator. Chocolate is made from the beans of the cacao tree, whose pods grow straight out of its trunk. Bananas first grew wild in rainforests in South-East Asia. Vanilla is the dried brown pod of an orchid vine from Mexico. Brazil nuts are gathered from giant wild trees in the Amazon, which only make nuts in forest, because big forest bees open their flowers and agoutis bury the nuts that grow into new trees.
familyTip: At snack time, play 'rainforest or not?' with what is on the table: a banana or a chocolate biscuit is a yes, an apple or a cheese sandwich is a no. Look for the word cocoa or vanilla on a wrapper, and find Brazil, Mexico or Ghana on a map or globe together.

visual.caption: Do we eat the fruit or the seeds? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: sort foods by their plant, take a cacao pod to chocolate, match foods to plants, help a Brazil nut tree, find rainforest foods in a lunchbox.

kid: A rainforest is a big forest where it is hot and wet all year. Lots of the food in your kitchen came from rainforest plants first. Chocolate, bananas, vanilla and Brazil nuts all did. Apples, carrots and bread did not. They grow in cool fields.

Chocolate grows on a tree! The cacao tree has big pods that grow right on its trunk. Inside each pod are lots of beans. People take the beans out and let them rest. Then they dry them in the sun, roast them, and grind them up with sugar. Now it is chocolate. Cows do not make chocolate.
Vanilla comes from a plant that climbs up trees. Its long thin pods start green. Then they are dried until they are dark brown. Bananas grow in a big bunch on a plant with giant leaves.

Brazil nuts grow high up on giant trees, inside a hard ball. The tree needs big bees from the forest to open its flowers. Then an animal called an agouti buries some nuts. The ones it forgets grow into new trees. So Brazil nuts need the whole forest.
adult: Ages 5 to 7. This links KS1 science (plants: name and describe common plants and their parts) with KS1 geography (hot areas of the world near the equator). A tropical rainforest is hot and wet all year, with rain in every month. Cacao (Theobroma cacao) is native to the Amazon basin; people in Central and South America made cacao drinks thousands of years ago. Its flowers and pods grow straight from the trunk and older branches, and a pod holds about 20 to 60 seeds (Britannica). Today about half or more of the world's cocoa is grown in Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana (ICCO). Key words: rainforest, equator, cacao, pod, bean, seed, orchid, vine, pollinate.

Cocoa processing (ICCO): farmers cut the ripe pods, scoop out the beans with their white pulp, and leave them to ferment for about 5 to 7 days under banana leaves or in boxes. They then sun-dry them for about a week. Factories roast and crack the beans, grind the nibs into cocoa mass, and mix it with sugar (and milk for milk chocolate). Vanilla (Vanilla planifolia) is a climbing orchid from the forests of Mexico and Central America. Its green pods are cured for months until they turn dark brown. The tiny black specks in vanilla ice cream are its seeds. Bananas descend from wild plants of South-East Asian tropical forests and are now farmed across the tropics.

Brazil nut trees (Bertholletia excelsa) grow up to about 50 metres tall in the Amazon. Their flowers have a heavy hood that only large, strong bees can push open, and those bees depend on the surrounding forest. Trees left alone in cleared land or planted in plantations make few nuts, so almost all Brazil nuts are gathered from wild forest. Each hard fruit holds about 10 to 25 nuts. Agoutis gnaw the fruit open and bury the nuts, and the forgotten ones grow into new trees (Mori and Prance 1990; Kew).

Common mistakes: thinking chocolate comes from milk or even brown cows (in a 2017 US survey, 7% of adults said chocolate milk comes from brown cows); thinking vanilla is white because vanilla ice cream is; thinking foods grow near where we buy them; and thinking any tree will fruit on its own, anywhere. Be careful not to say every banana or bar of chocolate comes from a rainforest today: many are grown on farms in hot, wet places, sometimes where forest was cleared. In the lab your child sorts 8 foods, puts 5 cacao steps in order, matches 4 foods to their plants, helps a Brazil nut tree with a forest, a bee and an agouti, and finds the rainforest foods in a lunchbox.

practice.hint: Think about the pods on the tree trunk in the lab.
practice.explain: Chocolate is made from cacao beans. They grow in pods on a rainforest tree. Sugar, and sometimes milk, are added at the end.

practice.prompt: A cacao tree has {a} pods on its trunk and {b} pods on a thick branch. How many pods is that?
practice.hint: Start with the pods on the trunk, then count on the pods on the branch.
practice.explain: {a} pods and {b} more pods make {=a+b} pods. Cacao pods grow right on the trunk and the thick branches.

practice.prompt: A bunch has {a} bananas. You eat 1. How many bananas are left?
practice.hint: Take 1 away from the number in the bunch.
practice.explain: {a} take away 1 leaves {=a-1} bananas. Bananas grow in a bunch on a plant with giant leaves.

practice.prompt: Which of these comes from a rainforest plant?
practice.hint: Which one grows on a plant that climbs up trees in a hot, wet forest?
practice.explain: Vanilla comes from the pods of an orchid vine from rainforests in Mexico. Apples and carrots grow in cool places.

practice.prompt: What colour are vanilla pods when they are ready to use?
practice.hint: They start green on the vine, and then they are dried for a long time.
practice.explain: Dark brown. Vanilla pods are dried for months. Vanilla ice cream is pale because of the cream, not the vanilla.

pool.hint: Picture the cacao tree in the lab.
pool.explain: Cacao pods grow straight out of the trunk and thick branches of the cacao tree.

pool.prompt: What happens to cacao beans before they are roasted?
pool.hint: Farmers spread the beans out where it is hot and bright.
pool.explain: The beans rest for a few days, then dry in the sun for about a week. After that they are roasted and ground with sugar.

pool.prompt: You open a cacao pod. You take out {a} beans, then {b} more. How many beans did you take out?
pool.hint: Start at {a} and count on {b} more.
pool.explain: {a} beans and {b} more make {=a+b} beans. One pod can hold 20 to 60 beans.

pool.prompt: Who helps Brazil nut flowers make nuts?
pool.hint: The flower has a heavy lid. Who is strong enough to push it open?
pool.explain: Big, strong bees from the forest push the heavy lid open and carry pollen. Then the nuts can grow.

pool.prompt: Who plants new Brazil nut trees?
choices: The wind that blows the nuts
pool.hint: Think about the animal that saves nuts to eat later.
pool.explain: Agoutis bury nuts to eat later. The nuts they forget grow into new Brazil nut trees.

pool.prompt: Your lunchbox has {a} foods from rainforest plants and {b} other foods. How many foods are in your lunchbox?
pool.hint: Add the rainforest foods and the other foods together.
pool.explain: {a} rainforest foods and {b} other foods make {=a+b} foods in all.

pool.prompt: A Brazil nut tree stands alone in a field. Why does it make hardly any nuts?
choices: The big bees live in the forest
pool.hint: What does the tree need to open its flowers, and where does it live?
pool.explain: With no forest, the big bees do not come, so the flowers are not opened and few nuts grow. Brazil nuts need the forest.

pool.prompt: Where did bananas first grow wild?
pool.hint: Banana plants like it hot and wet all year.
pool.explain: Bananas first grew wild in hot, wet rainforests in South-East Asia. Now farmers grow them in hot places all over the world.
